topic.examWeightHint: FM1 is a single 2-hour calculator paper of 100 marks. Forming and solving three equations is the long question near the end of the paper, set every year read (Summer 2018 Q10, 2021 Q11, 2022 Q11, 2023 Q11, 2024 Q11, 2025 Q12) for 11 to 14 marks. The stem names the three letters and their units. Short parts then form one equation or show that the information gives a printed one, for 1 or 2 marks each: comparisons sit inside the totals (2022: £8 dearer, 50% dearer), groups can be fractions of others (2021: two thirds, 25 more, half), and the printed form is reached by dividing (2024: 'Divide by 2', 'Divide by 3', MW1 each). The Teacher Guidance says sole use of a calculator gains no marks.

sheet.howExamined: FM1 is a single 2-hour calculator paper of 100 marks. Forming and solving three equations is the long question near the end of the paper, set every year read (Summer 2018 Q10, 2021 Q11, 2022 Q11, 2023 Q11, 2024 Q11, 2025 Q12) for 11 to 14 marks. The stem names the three letters and their units. Short parts then form one equation or show that the information gives a printed one, for 1 or 2 marks each: comparisons sit inside the totals (2022: £8 dearer, 50% dearer), groups can be fractions of others (2021: two thirds, 25 more, half), and the printed form is reached by dividing (2024: 'Divide by 2', 'Divide by 3', MW1 each). An 8-mark part solves the three equations with each stage shown (2024: M1 W1 for each elimination, then the values), and a final step returns to the context: multiplying thousands back up (2024), a reverse percentage and a currency conversion (2025 Q12(iv)). The Teacher Guidance says sole use of a calculator gains no marks.
traps: Translating 'dearer' and 'per cent greater' into algebra: the Summer 2022 report found many unable to write '£8 dearer' or '50% greater' as an expression (Q11); a percentage multiplies, 1 + p/100.
Starting from a percentage slip: the Summer 2023 report found incorrect first equations, 'possibly confused by the percentage signs' (Q11).
Dividing the two sides of an equation by different numbers to reach the printed form (Summer 2023 FM1 Q11).
Multiplying instead of dividing to reach each given equation, and thousands on the right-hand side causing problems (Summer 2024 FM1 Q11).
Working backwards from the given equation, which limited the method marks (Summer 2025 FM1 Q12); a show-that runs forwards.
Leaving a letter out of an equation, especially with a count of one (Summer 2025 FM1 Q12: variables omitted).
Solving in thousands and never multiplying by 1000 for the final mark (Summer 2024 FM1 Q11).
The final context step: Summer 2025 FM1 Q12(iv) was the part of that paper answered least well; many did not allow for the 40% decrease or chose another rate.
Accepting very large or negative values without question, and an unscaffolded equation such as x + y - z = 55 written for 'z is £55 more than x and y together' (Summer 2018 FM1 Q10).
Values produced on a calculator with no method, which gained no marks (Summer 2024 FM1 Q11, Summer 2025 FM1 Q12).
Leaving values as fractions where the context wants decimals or money, which lost the final mark (Summer 2025 FM1 Q12).

noteBlocks.lede: Three unknown prices, counts or rates, and three pieces of information about them. Each piece becomes one equation, the paper usually prints the tidy form for you to reach, and then the solving is the method you know. Most of the marks are in the forming.

Solve with every stage shown, then answer in the context's units.

noteBlocks.md: The question names the three letters and their units for you: in the drawing, $x$, $y$ and $z$ are numbers of adult, child and senior tickets. Each total the question gives is one equation. Every group contributes its count times its price, and the groups add up to the total.

The letters can be counts, as here, or prices with the counts given: the Summer 2021 paper counted passengers at known fares, and 2022 priced car hire. Either way, every letter the total involves appears in its equation, even with a count of one.

noteBlocks.title: Why three pieces of information
noteBlocks.md: One equation in three letters is true for endless triples: $9x + 5y + 6z = 1290$ holds for 80, 60 and 45 tickets and for 100, 30 and 40. Each further piece of information rules triples out, and three that say different things leave exactly one.

noteBlocks.stem: A cinema sells adult, child and senior tickets at £9, £5 and £6. On Friday it sold $x$ adult, $y$ child and $z$ senior tickets, and took £1290. Write down an equation in $x$, $y$ and $z$.

steps.decision: Each of the $x$ adult tickets costs £9, so they bring in $9 \times x$.
The same for each group: its price times its count, in pounds.
The three groups together make Friday's takings, in pounds on both sides.

noteBlocks.prompt: A bakery sells loaves at £2.40, cakes at £3.10 and pies at £4.50. On Saturday it sold $x$ loaves, $y$ cakes and $z$ pies and took £516.60. Which equation says that?
noteBlocks.explain: As in the takings bar, each group brings in its count times its price: $2.4x$ from loaves, $3.1y$ from cakes and $4.5z$ from pies, all in pounds. Their total is the takings, so $2.4x+3.1y+4.5z=516.6$. Keep one unit on both sides.

optionNotes.why: This adds the numbers of items sold, as if every item cost £1; each count has to be multiplied by its own price.
The prices are in pence on the left and the takings in pounds on the right, so the two sides are in different units.

twin.prompt: A garden centre sells trays of basil, mint and thyme at £3, £4 and £6. One day it sold $x$, $y$ and $z$ trays and took £330. Which equation says that?
twin.explain: Each count times its price, in pounds: $3x+4y+6z=330$.

optionNotes.why: This counts trays; each count has to be multiplied by its price.
Pence on the left and pounds on the right: the sides are in different units.

noteBlocks.md: Comparisons change a letter before it goes into a total. A fixed amount adds: "£8 dearer" turns $x$ into $x + 8$. A percentage is different, because it is a share of the letter itself. In the drawing, "40% dearer" adds $0.4z$ to $z$, so the new charge is $1.4z$: a percentage rise multiplies by $1 + \frac{p}{100}$.
That is why $z + 40$ can never be right. It adds £40 whatever $z$ is, while 40% of a small charge is small and 40% of a large one is large.

noteBlocks.stem: A small van's insurance is $z$ pounds a day. A large van's insurance is 40% dearer. Write the large van's daily insurance in terms of $z$.

steps.decision: The percentage is of the small van's charge, so it is a multiple of z.
Dearer means the extra is added to the small van's charge.
Collect: one $z$ and $0.4$ of a $z$ make $1.4z$, the multiplier $1 + \frac{40}{100}$.
A check with a number: £15 plus 40% of £15, which is £6, is £21.

noteBlocks.prompt: A car's fuel charge is $y$ pounds a mile. For a luxury car it is 30% greater. Which expression is the luxury car's charge?
noteBlocks.explain: 30% of $y$ is $0.3y$, a share of the charge itself, just as the extra piece of the bar was $0.4z$. Greater adds it on: $y + 0.3y = 1.3y$. A fixed number added to $y$ would be the same whatever $y$ was, which a percentage never is.

optionNotes.why: The 30 is added as pounds, but a percentage is a share of y, so it has to multiply.
This adds 30p whatever the charge is; 30% of y depends on y.

twin.prompt: A room costs $x$ pounds a night. A suite costs 25% more. Which expression is the suite's price?

optionNotes.why: That adds £25; the 25% is a share of x.
That is only the extra; the suite costs the room's price plus it.

noteBlocks.md: On the paper the comparisons arrive inside a total, as in Summer 2022: a Standard car's hire was £8 dearer than an Economy car's and its insurance 50% dearer, and then the cost of a whole rental was given. Replace each letter by its changed form, multiply by the days or the miles, collect the numbers, then divide to the printed form.

noteBlocks.stem: For a small van, $x$ is the daily hire charge, $y$ the charge per mile and $z$ the daily insurance, all in pounds. A large van's daily hire is £12 dearer, its charge per mile is the same and its daily insurance is 20% dearer. A large van for 10 days and 600 miles costs £690. Show that $5x + 300y + 6z = 285$.

steps.working: large van: hire $x+12$, insurance $1.2z$ a day
steps.decision: The fixed amount adds; the percentage multiplies.
Ten days of hire and insurance, 600 miles at y a mile.
Expand, and take the 120 from the hire across to the other side.
Every term divides by 2, the right-hand side too: this is the printed line.

noteBlocks.prompt: A coach costs $x$ pounds a day to hire. A minibus costs £15 a day less. Which expression is the cost of hiring the minibus for 4 days?
noteBlocks.explain: Change the letter first, then multiply, as the large van's hire became $x + 12$ before it was multiplied by 10. The minibus is $x - 15$ a day, so 4 days cost $4(x - 15) = 4x - 60$. The difference is taken off once for every day.

optionNotes.why: The £15 comes off every day, so over 4 days it comes off four times.
Less means the difference is taken away from the coach's charge, not added.

twin.prompt: A single room costs $x$ pounds a night and a double costs £25 more. Which expression is the cost of 5 nights in a double?
twin.explain: A double is $x + 25$ a night, so 5 nights cost $5(x + 25) = 5x + 125$.

optionNotes.why: The extra £25 is paid every night, so five times.
More is added to the single room's price, not taken away.

noteBlocks.md: A "show that" prints the equation you must reach, and the marks are for reaching it. Form your own equation from the information first. Then compare one of its coefficients with the printed one: if the printed one is smaller, divide every term by the factor, the right-hand side included.

noteBlocks.title: What the reports found
noteBlocks.md: Summer 2024: some candidates multiplied where the step to each given equation was a division, and many found the thousands on the right-hand side hard to handle. Summer 2023: some candidates divided the two sides of an equation by different numbers. Summer 2025: working backwards from the given answer limited the method marks.

noteBlocks.stem: Bank A pays $x$% interest a year, bank B pays $y$% and bank C pays $z$%. Ruth deposits £2500 in A, £4000 in B and £1500 in C, and receives £290 interest in a year. Show that $5x + 8y + 3z = 58$.

steps.decision: A rate of $x$% on £2500 earns $\frac{x}{100}$ of it. The same gives $40y$ and $15z$.
The three amounts of interest make the £290.
Compare 25 with the printed 5: divide every term by 5, and 290 by 5 too.

noteBlocks.prompt: Your equation is $24x + 36y + 60z = 480$ and the printed form is $2x + 3y + 5z = 40$. Which step takes yours to the printed one?
noteBlocks.explain: Compare one coefficient: 24 becomes 2, so the factor is 12 and the step is a division, as 25 became 5 in the boxes. The same factor must work on every term and on the right-hand side: $480 \div 12 = 40$. If one factor does not fit all four numbers, the line above has a slip.

optionNotes.why: The printed coefficients are smaller than yours, so multiplying moves away from them.
An equation stays true only if both sides change together, so 480 is divided by 12 as well.

twin.prompt: Your equation is $35x + 14y + 21z = 245$ and the printed form is $5x + 2y + 3z = 35$. Which step takes yours to the printed one?
twin.explain: 35 becomes 5, so divide every term by 7, and $245 \div 7 = 35$.

optionNotes.why: The printed numbers are smaller, so the step is a division.
The 245 has to be divided by 7 too.

noteBlocks.md: When the letters are in thousands of pounds, every amount of money in the equation must be in thousands too: £28 000 is written as 28. The Summer 2024 report found the thousands hard to handle, and many who solved correctly lost the last mark by never multiplying by 1000.

noteBlocks.stem: A kitchen fitter's profits are $x$, $y$ and $z$ thousand pounds on a small, a medium and a large kitchen. In May she fitted 6 small, 4 medium and 2 large kitchens for a total profit of £28 000. Show that $3x + 2y + z = 14$.

steps.decision: Put the total in the letters' unit before writing the equation.
Each count times its profit, in thousands on both sides.
Every term divides by 2, the 28 too: the printed line.

noteBlocks.prompt: With the same letters, in June she fitted 9 small, 6 medium and 3 large kitchens for a total profit of £42 000. Which equation says that?
noteBlocks.explain: Put the total into the letters' unit first, as £28 000 became 28: £42 000 is 42 thousand. Then each count times its profit: $9x + 6y + 3z = 42$. Dividing is only allowed when every term, the 42 included, is divided.

optionNotes.why: The letters are in thousands, so the total must be too: £42 000 is 42.
The left-hand side has been divided by 3 and the 42 has not.

twin.prompt: In July she fitted 8 small, 2 medium and 6 large kitchens for £44 000. Which equation says that?

optionNotes.why: Thousands on the left and pounds on the right.
Only the left-hand side has been halved.

noteBlocks.text: See it done: the solve at exam length

noteBlocks.md: The solving part prints three equations and asks for every stage: the Teacher Guidance says sole use of a calculator gains no marks. Clear the same letter from two pairs, solve that pair, go back for the third value, check it in the equation you did not use, and finish in the question's units.

noteBlocks.stem: With the same letters, the fitter's three months give $(1)$ $4x + 5y + 3z = 32$, $(2)$ $3x + 5y + 2z = 26$ and $(3)$ $3x + 2y + z = 14$. Solve them, showing each stage, and give each profit in pounds.

steps.decision: $z$ has a coefficient of 1 in $(3)$, so it is the easiest letter to clear.
Clear the same letter, $z$, from a second pair, or the two new equations will not match.
Write the first as $5x + y = 10$ and take away the second: $y$ goes.
Back through $5x + y = 10$, then $(3)$.
Check in an equation not used last; then scale back: £1500, £2500 and £4500.

noteBlocks.title: Simultaneous Equations with Three Unknowns in a Context - Corbettmaths
noteBlocks.why: Another context, formed and solved at writing speed. Pause after each equation is written and say where it came from.

noteBlocks.prompt: Using $(3)$ $2x + y + z = 9$, you clear $z$ from $(1)$ $5x + 3y + 4z = 29$. Which equation do you reach?
noteBlocks.explain: $(1) - 4 \times (3)$: the $4z$ terms match, so subtracting clears them, as $3 \times (3)$ cleared $3z$ above. Every term of $(3)$ is multiplied by 4, the 9 included: $5x + 3y + 4z - 8x - 4y - 4z = 29 - 36$, so $-3x - y = -7$, which is $3x + y = 7$.

optionNotes.why: Here the 9 was never multiplied by 4, so the right-hand side is out of step with the left.
Adding makes the $z$ terms bigger; to clear $4z$ with $4z$ you subtract.

twin.prompt: Using $(3)$ $x + 2y + z = 8$, you clear $z$ from $(1)$ $3x + 5y + 2z = 21$. Which equation do you reach?

optionNotes.why: The 8 was not doubled along with the rest of (3).
Adding keeps the z terms; subtract to clear them.

noteBlocks.text: When an answer cannot be true

noteBlocks.md: Read the three values as the things they stand for before you write them on the answer lines. The Summer 2018 report found candidates accepting very large or negative values as if they meant something. A negative count or an impossible price is a message about the equations: most often one comparison was written back to front, and the solving then worked faithfully on it.

noteBlocks.stem: A cycle club has $x$ adult, $y$ junior and $z$ senior members, paying £20, £12 and £8 a year. It has 66 members, there are 20 more junior members than senior members, and the fees total £1100. Solving a candidate's equations gave $x = 48$, $y = -1$, $z = 19$. Find the slip and the true numbers.

steps.decision: A club cannot have a negative number of members, so an equation is at fault, not the arithmetic.
Check each equation against its own sentence.
The juniors are the larger group, so their letter stands alone.
Solve the corrected equations.

noteBlocks.stem: The curve $y = ax^{2} + bx + c$ passes through $(1, 4)$, $(2, 9)$ and $(-1, 6)$. Find $a$, $b$ and $c$.

steps.decision: One equation per point: $x^{2}$ multiplies $a$ and $x$ multiplies $b$.
The a and c terms match in (1) and (3), so one subtraction clears both.
From $(1)$. The curve is $y = 2x^{2} - x + 3$; check at $(2, 9)$: $8 - 2 + 3 = 9$.

noteBlocks.prompt: The curve $y = ax^{2} + bx + c$ passes through $(-2, 11)$. Which equation does that point give?
noteBlocks.explain: Substitute $x = -2$ and $y = 11$: $a(-2)^{2} + b(-2) + c = 11$. The square is positive, $4a$, but the single $x$ keeps its sign, $-2b$, just as $x = -1$ gave $a - b + c$. So $4a - 2b + c = 11$.

optionNotes.why: Squaring $-2$ gives $+4$, so the $a$ term is $4a$.
The $b$ term is $b$ times $x$, and $x$ is $-2$, so it is $-2b$.

twin.prompt: The same kind of curve passes through $(-3, 20)$. Which equation does that point give?

optionNotes.why: $bx$ with $x = -3$ is $-3b$.

items.stem:
Four quick checks on what this lesson is built from. None of them is the new work, so answer from what you already know.
A price of £3.60 rises by 35%. What is the new price?
items.skill: Prerequisite: a percentage increase as a multiplier

options.feedback: A rise of 35% multiplies by $1.35$: $1.35 \times 3.6 = 4.86$.
That adds 35 pounds. A percentage is a share of the price, so it multiplies.
That adds 35p. The 35% is 35% of £3.60, not a fixed amount.

items.stem: Ciarán is $y$ years old. Dermot is 7 years older than Ciarán. How old is Dermot, in terms of $y$?
items.skill: Prerequisite: writing a comparison in algebra

options.feedback: Older means more, so the difference is added to the younger one's age.
That makes Dermot the younger. Decide who is older before choosing the sign.
'Older than' is a difference, so it is added; 7y would be seven times as old.

items.stem: How many pence are there in £13.40?
items.skill: Prerequisite: converting between pounds and pence

options.feedback: Multiply by 100. One unit throughout keeps the coefficients whole.
That multiplies by ten; there are 100 pence in a pound.
That multiplies by a thousand, ten times too many.

items.stem: The curve $y = ax^{2} + bx + c$ passes through $(4, 50)$. What does the first term become when the point is substituted in?
items.skill: Prerequisite: substituting a value into a squared term

options.feedback: $x$ is squared before it multiplies $a$, and $4^{2} = 16$.
The square has been missed: the term is a x squared.
That is the $y$-coordinate, which belongs on the other side of the equals sign.

items.stem: A deluxe room costs 15% more than a standard room, which costs $y$ pounds. Which expression is the price of a deluxe room?

options.feedback: A rise of 15% is a multiplier of 1.15.
That adds 15 pounds whatever the room costs.
That is only the extra; the deluxe room costs the standard price plus it.

items.stem: A candidate writes $4x + 2y = 9.7$ for an order of 4 teas, 2 buns and 1 tray bake costing £9.70, where $x$, $y$ and $z$ are their prices in pounds. What is missing?
items.skill: Check every letter appears in the equation

options.feedback: A count of one still needs its letter. The Summer 2025 report found variables omitted.
The order includes a tray bake, so its price belongs in the bill: $4x + 2y + z = 9.7$.
The unit was fixed when the letters were named. The missing piece is a letter.

items.stem: Your equation is $18x + 12y + 6z = 144$ and the printed form is $3x + 2y + z = 24$. What is the step between them?
items.skill: Reach a printed form by scaling the whole equation

options.feedback: $18 \div 6 = 3$, and the same factor works on all four numbers.
The printed coefficients are smaller, so multiplying moves away from them.

options.text: Divide only the left-hand side by 6
options.feedback: Both sides change together, or the equation stops being true.

items.stem: A show-that question prints the equation you have to reach. Where does the working start?

options.text: At the information in the question, finishing at the printed line
options.feedback: The derivation is what carries the marks, so it has to run forwards. The printed line is your last line, never your first.

options.text: At the printed equation, checking that the information fits it
options.feedback: That is working backwards, and it gains nothing: examiners have said so in more than one series.

options.text: At the answers, substituting them into the printed equation
options.feedback: The answers are not known yet at this stage, and substituting a result is verification rather than derivation.

items.stem: The letters are in thousands of pounds and the solving gives $y = 3.4$. The question asks for the profit in pounds. What do you write?

options.feedback: Multiply by 1000: each unit of y is one thousand pounds.
That is the value in thousands; the scaling back is a mark of its own.
The scaling has been applied twice.

items.stem: Solving for the numbers of three kinds of coin in a jar gives 46, 71 and −9. What should come next?

options.text: Go back and check the equations formed

Changing one value leaves the faulty equation, so the other two values stay unreliable.

parts.workedSolution:
The coffee is the dearer of the two, so its price is the scone's price plus the difference.

commonErrors.feedback: That makes the scone the dearer of the two. Read the sentence again and ask which price the extra is added to: it is the coffee, so the coffee's letter sits on its own.

A café sells scones, coffees and bowls of soup.
Let $x$ be the price of a scone, $y$ the price of a coffee and $z$ the price of a bowl of soup, all in pounds.

An order of 2 scones, 3 coffees and 1 bowl of soup costs £12.25.

Write down an equation in $x$, $y$ and $z$.

Answer ________

scheme.for: each item's count multiplied by its own letter and the three terms added

hints: Count of an item times the price of that item gives what that part of the order costs.
All three letters belong in the equation, even the one whose count is one.
parts.workedSolution:
The scones cost $2x$, the coffees $3y$ and the soup $z$.
Adding them gives the bill, so $2x + 3y + z = 12.25$.
A check with the real prices: $2.8 + 6.3 + 3.15 = 12.25$.

commonErrors.feedback: The soup has been left out. Its count is one, so its term is simply $z$, and an equation missing a letter cannot be solved with the others.
That is the bill for one of each. The counts multiply their own letters, so the scones contribute $2x$ and the coffees $3y$.

questions.solutionProgram: order 2 scones, 3 coffees, 1 soup -> 2x + 3y + z = 12.25; check 2x1.4 + 3x2.1 + 3.15 = 12.25

context.setting: A counting comparison in a jar of coins

parts.stem:
A charity jar holds twenty-pence coins, fifty-pence coins and one-pound coins.
Let $x$ be the number of twenty-pence coins, $y$ the number of fifty-pence coins and $z$ the number of one-pound coins.

There are as many twenty-pence coins as there are fifty-pence and one-pound coins together.

Write down an equation in $x$, $y$ and $z$.

Answer ________

scheme.for: the two smaller groups added together on one side
$x = y + z$, or any equation equivalent to it such as $x - y - z = 0$

hints: "As many as" is an equals sign.
Together means added, so the two counts on that side are joined by a plus.
parts.workedSolution:
"As many as" is an equals sign, and "together" adds the two counts on the other side.
That gives $x = y + z$, which can also be written $x - y - z = 0$.
A check with the real counts: $15 + 9 = 24$.

commonErrors.feedback: The grouping has moved. The sentence puts the twenty-pence coins on their own and the other two together, so the plus sign belongs on the far side of the equals sign.
That says all three counts are the same, which the sentence does not. Only the twenty-pence count matches the other two added together.

questions.solutionProgram: x = y + z -> x - y - z = 0; check 24 = 15 + 9

emphasis: a point substituted into a curve

context.setting: One point of a curve turned into an equation in its coefficients

parts.stem:
A curve has the equation $y = ax^2 + bx + c$.

The curve passes through the point $(2, 15)$.

Write down an equation in $a$, $b$ and $c$.

Answer ________

scheme.for: substituting $x = 2$ and $y = 15$ into $y = ax^2 + bx + c$

hints: The point gives you a value of $x$ and a value of $y$; put both into the equation of the curve.
$x^2$ becomes $4$, so the first term is $4a$.
parts.workedSolution:
Substituting $x = 2$ and $y = 15$ gives $a(2)^2 + b(2) + c = 15$.
Working out the numbers, $4a + 2b + c = 15$.
A check with the real coefficients: $8 + 6 + 1 = 15$.

commonErrors.feedback: The two coordinates have swapped places. The first number of a pair is $x$, which is the one that goes into $x^2$ and $bx$; the second is $y$, which is the total.
The substitution is right, so the method mark stands. The first term is $a x^2$, so $x = 2$ makes it $4a$, not $2a$.

questions.solutionProgram: point (2, 15) in y = ax^2 + bx + c -> 4a + 2b + c = 15

$x = y + 5$, or any equation equivalent to it such as $x - y = 5$

hints: Which sister is the older one? Her age is the other's plus the difference.
Check your equation with any pair of ages that fits the sentence.
parts.workedSolution:

That can also be written $x - y = 5$.
A check with the real ages: $17 - 12 = 5$.

commonErrors.feedback: That makes Bróna the elder. Whoever the sentence says is older has the plus added to the other one's age, so Aoife's letter sits on its own.

hints: Read the definition of the letters again; they are not in pounds.
One thousand pounds for every $1$ of $x$.

emphasis: a reverse percentage after the solving is done

context.setting: A profit after a fall, with the profit before it wanted

parts.stem:
A printing firm takes standard, premium and bespoke orders.
Let $x$ be the profit on a standard order, $y$ the profit on a premium order and $z$ the profit on a bespoke order, each in thousands of pounds.

This year the profit on a bespoke order is £3500. That is 30% less than it was last year.

Calculate the profit on a bespoke order last year.

Answer £ ________

scheme.for: recognising this year's figure as $0.7$ of last year's
dividing: $3500 \div 0.7$

hints: A fall of 30% leaves 70% behind, which is a multiplier of $0.7$.
You are going backwards through that multiplication, so the step is a division.
Check your answer forwards before you write it down.
parts.workedSolution:
A fall of 30% leaves 70% of last year's profit, so this year's figure is $0.7$ times last year's.
Going backwards through that multiplication is a division: $3500 \div 0.7 = 5000$.
Check forwards: $5000 \times 0.7 = 3500$, so last year's profit was £5000.

commonErrors.feedback: That takes another 30% off this year's figure, so it goes further down when the answer has to be larger than £3500. Going backwards through a fall is a division.
Adding 30% back on is not the reverse of taking 30% off, because the percentage is of a different amount each time. Check forwards: $4550 \times 0.7$ does not come back to £3500.

parts.stem:
Aoife, Bróna and Ciara are sisters.
Let $x$ be Aoife's age, $y$ Bróna's age and $z$ Ciara's age, each in whole years.

Their three ages add to 37. Aoife is 5 years older than Bróna. Bróna and Ciara's ages add to 20.

Form three equations and solve them to find Aoife's age.
Set out every stage of your solution.

Answer ________ years

scheme.for: all three equations formed: $x + y + z = 37$, $x - y = 5$ and $y + z = 20$
one letter cleared from a pair of the equations
the two-unknown pair solved

hints: Write one equation per sentence before you try to solve anything.
Equation $(3)$ already has no $x$ in it, so it is halfway to being the pair you need.
Taking equation $(3)$ from equation $(1)$ leaves an equation in $x$ alone.
parts.workedSolution:
The three sentences give $(1)$ $x + y + z = 37$, $(2)$ $x - y = 5$ and $(3)$ $y + z = 20$.
Equation $(3)$ contains no $x$, so subtracting it from $(1)$ leaves $x = 17$ directly.
So Aoife is 17 years old.

commonErrors.feedback: That reads the third sentence as giving Bróna's age. It says Bróna **and Ciara's** ages add to 20, so equation $(3)$ is $y + z = 20$ and 20 is not an age on its own.

parts.stem:
Write down Bróna's age.

Answer ________ years
hints: Substitute Aoife's age into equation $(2)$.

parts.stem:
Write down Ciara's age.

Answer ________ years
hints: Substitute Bróna's age into equation $(3)$.

A bowl of soup costs 50% more than a coffee.

Write down an equation in $y$ and $z$.

Answer ________

hints: A rise of 50% multiplies by $1.5$.

parts.stem:
An order of 2 scones, 3 coffees and 1 bowl of soup costs £12.25.

Write down an equation in $x$, $y$ and $z$.

Answer ________

scheme.for: each count multiplied by its own letter and the three terms added

hints: The soup's count is one, so its term is simply $z$; it still has to appear.
parts.workedSolution: The order costs $2x$ for the scones, $3y$ for the coffees and $z$ for the soup, so $2x + 3y + z = 12.25$.

parts.stem:
Set out every stage of your solution.

Solve your three equations to find the price of a scone.

Answer £ ________

scheme.for: one unknown removed, by eliminating it from a pair or by substituting one of the given equations, for example substituting $y = x + 0.7$ into the order equation
a correct equation in fewer unknowns
the working carried through to a single unknown

hints: Number the equations $(1)$, $(2)$ and $(3)$ before you touch them.
Two of your equations already give $y$ and $z$ in terms of the others, so substitution is quicker than elimination here.
Clear the same letter from a second pair, then solve the two equations you are left with.

From (a), $y = x + 0.7$. From (b), $z = 1.5y = 1.5(x + 0.7)$.
Substituting both into (c) gives $2x + 3(x + 0.7) + 1.5(x + 0.7) = 12.25$.
Collecting the terms, $6.5x + 3.15 = 12.25$, so $x = 1.4$.
A scone costs £1.4.

commonErrors.feedback: A scone at $£2.37$ beside a coffee at $£2.10$ is a signal in itself. That value comes from the comparison in (a) written the other way round, so check which of the two the sentence calls dearer.

parts.stem:
Write down the price of a coffee.

Answer £ ________

scheme.for: substituting the value already found back into an equation that still contains y

hints: One substitution is enough, and the other equation is then a free check.
parts.workedSolution: From (a), $y = 1.4 + 0.7 = 2.1$, so a coffee costs £2.1.

Answer £ ________

hints: Go back to an original equation, because the two you made no longer contain this letter.

From (b), $z = 1.5 \times 2.1 = 3.15$, so a bowl of soup costs £3.15.
Check in (c): $2.8 + 6.3 + 3.15 = 12.25$.

context.setting: A quadratic curve through three given points

parts.stem:
A curve has the equation $y = ax^2 + bx + c$.

It passes through the points $(1, 6)$, $(2, 15)$ and $(3, 28)$.

Write down the equation in $a$, $b$ and $c$ that comes from the point $(1, 6)$.

Answer ________

scheme.for: substituting $x = 1$ and $y = 6$ into $y = ax^2 + bx + c$

hints: The unknowns here are the three coefficients, not $x$ and $y$.
With $x = 1$ every coefficient is multiplied by one.
parts.workedSolution: Substituting $x = 1$ and $y = 6$ gives $a(1)^2 + b(1) + c = 6$, which is $a + b + c = 6$.

commonErrors.feedback: The two coordinates have swapped roles. The second number of the pair is the value of $y$, so it is the one on the right of the equals sign.

parts.stem:
Write down the equation that comes from the point $(2, 15)$.

Answer ________
hints: $x^2$ is $4$ here.
parts.workedSolution: Substituting gives $a(2)^2 + b(2) + c = 15$, which is $4a + 2b + c = 15$.

commonErrors.feedback: The first term carries $x^2$, so with $x = 2$ it is $4a$ rather than $2a$.

parts.stem:
Write down the equation that comes from the point $(3, 28)$.

Answer ________
hints: $x^2$ is $9$ here.
parts.workedSolution: Substituting gives $a(3)^2 + b(3) + c = 28$, which is $9a + 3b + c = 28$.

parts.stem:
Set out every stage of your solution.

Solve your three equations to find the value of $a$.
Set out every stage of your solution.

Answer ________

scheme.for: one unknown removed, by eliminating it from a pair or by substituting one of the given equations, for example $4a + 2b + c = 15$ minus $a + b + c = 6$
a correct equation in fewer unknowns
the working carried through to a single unknown

hints: Number the equations $(1)$, $(2)$ and $(3)$ before you touch them.
Every equation ends in $+ c$, so subtracting one from another clears $c$ at once.
Clear the same letter from a second pair, then solve the two equations you are left with.
parts.workedSolution:
Each equation ends in $+ c$, so subtracting clears it.
$(2) - (1)$ gives $3a + 1b = 9$, and $(3) - (2)$ gives $5a + 1b = 13$.
Subtracting those two leaves $2a = 4$, so $a = 2$.

commonErrors.feedback: That value comes from an equation whose $ax^2$ term was left out. Check that each of your three equations carries all three letters.

parts.stem:
Write down the value of $b$.

Answer ________
hints: One substitution is enough, and the other equation is then a free check.
parts.workedSolution: Substituting $a = 2$ into $3a + 1b = 9$ gives $b = 3$.

commonErrors.feedback: A negative coefficient is possible in general, and here it comes from a missing term rather than the algebra. Rebuild the equation from the point and try again.

parts.stem:
Write down the value of $c$.

Answer ________
hints: Go back to an original equation, because the two you made no longer contain this letter.

parts.stem:
Hence write down the equation of the curve.

Answer ________
hints: Put the three values you have found back into $y = ax^2 + bx + c$.
parts.workedSolution:
With $a = 2$, $b = 3$ and $c = 1$ the curve is $y = 2x^2 + 3x + 1$.
Check at $x = 3$: $18 + 9 + 1 = 28$.

commonErrors.feedback: The three values are right and two of them have changed places. $a$ is the coefficient of $x^2$ and $c$ is the number on its own.

reaching the printed form exactly

$(3) - (2)$ clears $x$: $-2y + 2z = 4$, which simplifies to $z - y = 2$.
Clearing $x$ from $(1)$ and $(2)$ as well and solving the pair gives $x = 2$ in thousands.
The letters are in thousands of pounds, so the profit on a standard order is $2 \times 1000 = £2000$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the value of $x$ in the units the letters were defined in. The question asks for pounds, so it still needs multiplying by $1000$. This is the step examiners report being forgotten after otherwise faultless solving.
A negative profit here is a signal rather than an answer. That value comes from the March equation scaled the wrong way in part (a), so check that the printed form was reached by dividing.

parts.stem:
Write down the profit on a premium order, in pounds.

Answer £ ________

scheme.for: substituting the value already found back into an equation that still contains y

hints: One substitution is enough, and the other equation is then a free check.
parts.workedSolution: Substituting back gives $y = 3$ in thousands, so the profit on a premium order is £3000.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the value of $y$ in thousands. Multiply by $1000$ to answer in pounds, as the question asks.

parts.stem:
Write down the profit on a bespoke order, in pounds.

Answer £ ________

scheme.for: substituting both known values into one of the original equations

hints: Go back to an original equation, because the two you made no longer contain this letter.
parts.workedSolution:
Substituting into $(2)$ gives $z = 5$ in thousands, so the profit on a bespoke order is £5000.
Check in $(1)$: $12 + 12 + 15 = 39$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the value of $z$ in thousands. The answer line asks for pounds, so it is $5 \times 1000$.

parts.stem:
The following year the profit on a bespoke order falls by 30%, to £3500.

Calculate the profit on a bespoke order in the year before that fall.

Answer £ ________

scheme.for: recognising £3500 as $0.7$ of the earlier profit

hints: A fall of 30% leaves 70% behind.
Going backwards through a multiplication is a division.
Your answer should agree with part (c)(iii), which is the check this part is really asking for.
parts.workedSolution:
A fall of 30% leaves 70% of the earlier profit, a multiplier of $0.7$.
So the earlier profit is $3500 \div 0.7 = 5000$.
That agrees with part (c)(iii), where the bespoke profit came out as £5000.

commonErrors.feedback: Taking another 30% off makes the figure smaller, and the answer has to be larger than £3500 because the profit fell. Reverse a fall by dividing.
Adding 30% back on is not the reverse of taking 30% off, because each percentage is of a different amount. Part (c)(iii) already gives the answer to check against.

context.setting: Three course prices described by a difference, a percentage and one order

parts.stem:
A drama school charges $x$, $y$ and $z$ pounds for a one-day, a two-day and a weekend course.
A two-day course costs £25 more than a one-day course.
A weekend course costs 80% more than a two-day course.
3 one-day courses, 2 two-day courses and 1 weekend course cost £503 altogether.
Form three equations and solve them to find the cost of a weekend course.

scheme.for: substituting to reach one unknown: $6.8x + 95 = 503$

hints: Two of the sentences give one price in terms of another: write those first.
Put $y = x + 25$ and $z = 1.8(x + 25)$ into the order.
Once x is known, work forwards through the comparisons.
parts.workedSolution:
The comparisons: $y = x + 25$ and $z = 1.8y$. The order: $3x + 2y + z = 503$.
Two equations already give a letter in terms of another, so substitute: $3x + 2(x + 25) + 1.8(x + 25) = 503$.
$6.8x + 95 = 503$, so $6.8x = 408$ and $x = 60$.
Then $y = 85$ and $z = 1.8 \times 85 = 153$: a weekend course costs £153. Check: $180 + 170 + 153 = 503$.

commonErrors.feedback: That comes from reading 80% more as £80 more. A percentage is a share of the two-day price, so the weekend course is $1.8y$, not $y + 80$. The difference, the order and the substitution still earn their marks.
That is the price of a one-day course. The question asks for the weekend course: carry on through the comparisons to z.

findTheMistake.stem: Seán is asked to show that a tea-room order gives $2x + 3y + z = 9$, where $x$, $y$ and $z$ are the prices in pounds of a pot of tea, a scone and a slice of cake. The order was 6 pots of tea, 9 scones and 3 slices of cake for £27. His working:
studentWorking: That matches 6 teas, 9 scones and 3 cakes for £27
So the printed equation is right
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Every line is true, and the whole still runs backwards. Line 1 starts from the printed equation, which is what had to be shown, and the rest only checks that it fits. A show-that is marked on the derivation: from the order to the printed line.
findTheMistake.feedback: Checking the printed equation against the order is verification, and the marks here are for deriving it. Start from the order, write 6x + 9y + 3z = 27, and divide every term by 3. The Summer 2025 report found working backwards from the answer limited the method marks.

findTheMistake.stem: Pádraig is told that a premium seat costs 60% more than a standard seat, where $y$ is the price of a standard seat and $z$ the price of a premium seat, both in pounds. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 turns a percentage into a fixed amount, and lines 2 and 3 follow honestly from it. 60% more is 60% of the standard price added on, so it multiplies: z = 1.6y. A premium seat at £85 beside a standard one at £25 should have been the signal.
findTheMistake.feedback: The percentage is of the standard price, so it depends on y and multiplies it. The Summer 2022 report found many candidates unable to translate '50% greater' into an algebraic expression.

findTheMistake.stem: A swimming club has $x$ adult, $y$ junior and $z$ senior members, paying £30, £18 and £12 a year. It has 43 members, there are 25 more junior members than senior members, and the fees total £900. Aisling's working:
studentWorking: So there are 22 adults, -2 juniors and 23 seniors
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The solving in line 4 is faithful to the equations it was given. Line 2 has the comparison back to front: the juniors are the larger group, so y = z + 25. Line 5 was the place to stop: no club has -2 members.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three equations and the method of solving earn their marks; the comparison is the slip. The Summer 2018 report found candidates accepting very large or negative values as if they meant something: a negative count sends you back to the equations.

prompts.prompt: How do you write "b costs 50% more than a" as an equation?
prompts.answer: b = 1.5a, because a rise of 50% multiplies by 1.5.

prompts.prompt: How do you write "b costs 70p more than a" as an equation, when the prices are in pounds?
prompts.answer: b = a + 0.7. The amount is added, and it is written in pounds to match the letters.

prompts.prompt: In a show-that question, which direction does the working run, and why?
prompts.answer: Forwards, from the information to the printed line. The derivation is what carries the marks, so starting at the printed equation earns nothing.

prompts.prompt: What are the stages of the forming-and-solving question?
prompts.answer: Form each equation, reach the printed form, solve, answer in context.

prompts.prompt: Your coefficients are larger than the printed ones. What do you do?
prompts.answer: Divide every term, the right-hand side too, by the same factor.

prompts.prompt: The letters are in thousands of pounds. What is the last step?
prompts.answer: Multiply each value by 1000 to answer in pounds.

prompts.prompt: Your solving gives a negative number of tickets. What does that tell you?
prompts.answer: An equation was formed from its sentence incorrectly: check each one.

prompts.prompt: How do you undo a fall of p%?
prompts.answer: Divide the new value by 1 − p/100.

findings.asked: Form three equations from a context (one not given as 'show that'), then solve.
findings.wentWrong: The unscaffolded equation was often wrong (x + y - z = 55 was typical); 'show' equations were set out poorly; wrong equations led to huge or negative values that were not questioned.
findings.rule: Translate each sentence separately and check the answers make sense.

findings.asked: Translate phrases like 'dearer' and '50% greater' into equations, then solve.
findings.wentWrong: The phrase-to-algebra steps were often omitted; the solving was excellent; money notation was rarely used.

findings.asked: Derive three given equations from percentages, then solve.
findings.wentWrong: Fewer worked backwards from the given equations than before, but starting equations were wrong (percentage signs confused) and sides were divided by different numbers to force the printed form; solving was near perfect.
findings.rule: Divide the whole equation by one number to reach the printed form.

findings.asked: Form equations in thousands, solve, then interpret.
findings.wentWrong: Multiplying instead of dividing to reach each given equation; an error in (i) propagated; after solving, many forgot to multiply by 1000; calculator-only answers earned nothing.
findings.rule: If you scaled down to solve, scale back up at the end - and show the method.

findings.asked: Form and solve three equations from a currency context, then reverse a 40% decrease.
findings.wentWrong: Variables were omitted from equations; some worked backwards from the answers; arithmetic slips; calculator jumps with no working; fractional answers; the final reverse-percentage-and-conversion step was the worst-answered part of the paper.
findings.rule: Write all three unknowns in every equation they belong to, solve on paper, and handle the final context step separately.

insight.ruleToRemember: Define x, y, z with units; turn each sentence into one equation; reach a printed form by dividing the whole equation by one number and show that line; after solving, rescale, answer in context and sanity-check the values.
insight.aStarSignal: Forming an unscaffolded equation from comparative wording and finishing with a context step (rescaling, a reverse percentage, a conversion).
